segments.label: 01 / 12 · HOOK
title: THE PARTICLE KILLED CELLS.
BUT DID IT REACH THE TUMOR?
segments.body_html:
targeted particle→kills cells in dish→tumor reached?

Cancer nanomedicine is not the study of clever particles. It is the study of where a particle goes and what it does when it gets there.

beats.text: A graduate student presents a poster. Her nanoparticle carries doxorubicin, targets a breast cancer receptor, and in cell culture kills tumor cells at one-tenth the usual dose. Then a reviewer asks one question: what percentage of your injected particles actually reached the tumor? She doesn't know. Nobody measured it. Cancer nanomedicine is not the study of clever particles. It is the study of where a particle goes and what it does when it gets there — and that requires measurement, not assumption.

segments.label: 02 / 12 · THE STAKES
title: CONVENTIONAL CHEMO
HITS EVERYTHING.
segments.body_html:
ALL
tissues exposed
→
TOXIC
collateral damage
→
DOSE
ceiling hit

The delivery problem is fundamental: concentrate drug where it is needed, minimize it where it is not.

beats.text: Conventional chemotherapy is a blunt tool. The bloodstream distributes drug throughout the body — bone marrow, gut lining, hair follicles, immune cells — and toxicity from this collateral exposure is what limits the dose a patient can receive. The fundamental promise of cancer nanomedicine is to concentrate drug at the tumor and spare healthy tissue. That promise is real. But delivering on it requires solving a chain of physical problems, and most particles in the literature fail that chain quietly.

segments.label: 03 / 12 · WHAT A NANOPARTICLE IS
title: SIZE IS NOT ENOUGH.
ENGINEERING IS WHAT COUNTS.
segments.body_html:
WATER0.3 nm
ANTIBODY10 nm
LIPOSOME10–200 nm · therapeutic window
An engineered nanoparticle: size · architecture · payload · surface · biodistribution — all deliberately specified.

beats.text: A nanoparticle is a particle with at least one dimension in the nanometer range — one to a thousand nanometers, with ten to two hundred being the clinically relevant window. A water molecule is 0.3 nanometers; a typical antibody is ten; a virus is twenty to three hundred; a red blood cell is seven thousand. But size alone is not what makes something nanomedicine. A small drug molecule a few nanometers wide is not nanomedicine. An engineered nanoparticle is one whose size, internal architecture, payload, and surface chemistry are deliberately specified to control its journey through the body. The engineering — not the smallness — is what counts.

segments.label: 04 / 12 · SIZE BEHAVIORS
title: THE 10–200 nm RANGE
DOES THINGS MOLECULES CANNOT.
segments.body_html:
TUMOR ACCUMULATIONLeaky tumor vessels let particles through; poor lymphatics trap them — the EPR effect.
LONG CIRCULATIONPEG coating resists opsonization; hours in blood vs. minutes for free drug.
PAYLOAD PROTECTIONsiRNA and mRNA survive seconds naked in blood — encapsulation buys the time to arrive.
MULTIFUNCTIONALITYOne particle: drug + imaging label + targeting ligand + triggered release.

beats.text: The ten-to-two-hundred nanometer range enables behaviors that free drug molecules cannot have. Tumor blood vessels are leakier than normal vasculature — particles in this size range escape through gaps and persist there because tumors drain poorly. This is the enhanced permeability and retention effect, or EPR. Coat a particle with polyethylene glycol and it evades the macrophages that would otherwise clear it, extending its time in circulation from minutes to hours. Encapsulate a therapeutic RNA and it survives the blood long enough to reach a cell. Pack a targeting ligand and an imaging tracer into the same object and you can track delivery and treat simultaneously. These are the engineering arguments for the field.

segments.label: 05 / 12 · THE DOSE-LOSS CHAIN
title: MOST OF WHAT IS INJECTED
NEVER ARRIVES.
segments.body_html:
injected dose→ survives circulation→ extravasates→ penetrates tissue→ cell uptake→ payload releases→ ~0.7% at target

A median of only about 0.7 percent of the injected dose reaches the tumor across published mouse studies.

beats.text: Between the syringe and the tumor cell's nucleus, dose is lost at every step. The particle must survive circulation — meaning not be cleared by the liver or spleen. Then it must escape the bloodstream into tumor tissue. Then penetrate the dense interstitium. Then be taken up by cells. Then release its payload. Then the payload must reach its molecular target. Fail at step three and you deliver nothing, no matter how elegantly step one was solved. The field's sobering published finding: across mouse studies, a median of only about 0.7 percent of the injected nanoparticle dose actually reaches the tumor. Most of what is injected does not arrive.

segments.label: 06 / 12 · CHARACTERIZATION
title: KNOW WHAT
YOU ACTUALLY BUILT.
segments.body_html:
SIZE & POLYDISPERSITYA wide spread means inconsistent in-vivo behavior — a 50 nm and a 300 nm particle take entirely different routes through the body.
SURFACE CHEMISTRYPEG that has aggregated, or a targeting peptide that detached during storage, is invisible to a cell-killing assay.
DRUG LOADING & RELEASEA particle releasing payload in the bloodstream is just delivering free drug with extra steps.
STABILITY & STERILITYDoes it hold together in serum, at physiological pH, and in storage?

beats.text: Before a particle can be claimed to do anything, its physical properties must be measured. A nanoparticle batch is not a single identical molecule — it is a population with a distribution of sizes, surface chemistries, and drug loadings. Polydispersity is not a cosmetic quality metric; it predicts in-vivo behavior, because a fifty-nanometer particle and a three-hundred-nanometer particle are cleared by different organs and extravasate with different efficiencies. Surface chemistry matters because a PEG coating that has aggregated, or a targeting peptide that detached in storage, is invisible to a cell-killing assay but decisive in an animal. Characterization is the step that connects 'we built this object' to 'we know what we built.'

segments.label: 07 / 12 · IMAGING DELIVERY
title: DELIVERY FAILURE
OR BIOLOGY FAILURE?
segments.body_html:
Delivery failureparticle never arrived — redesign the vehicle
⇄
Biology failureparticle arrived, target didn't respond — rethink the drug

Tumor volume alone cannot distinguish them. Only tracking the particle directly can.

beats.text: If a nanomedicine fails in a patient, there are two distinct explanations with opposite implications. Either the particle never arrived — a delivery failure — or it arrived and the target biology did not respond — a biology failure. These demand opposite fixes: redesign the particle, or rethink the drug. Tumor response alone cannot distinguish them. Labeling the particle with a tracer detectable by PET, MRI, or optical imaging allows direct tracking of biodistribution: how much accumulates in the tumor, how much in the liver and spleen, how the distribution changes over time. This measurement — not cell viability, not even tumor volume — is the evidence that a particle actually targeted something.

segments.label: 08 / 12 · TWO LIPOSOMES
title: IDENTICAL IN THE DISH,
OPPOSITE FATES IN THE BODY.
segments.body_html:
LAB A90 nm · tight distribution · PEGylated → long circulation · tumor accumulation · the Doxil logic
LAB Bavg 90 nm · wide spread (many >250 nm) · no PEG → rapidly opsonized · liver-cleared · fails the chain
Cell culture removes every step of the dose-loss chain where these two formulations differ. Judge on predicted biodistribution, not in-vitro potency.

beats.text: Consider two liposomal doxorubicin formulations. Lab A: ninety nanometers, tight size distribution, PEGylated. Lab B: average ninety nanometers but wide spread — many particles above two-fifty — no PEG coating. Same drug. Same average size. Same cell-killing in culture. The temptation is to call them equivalent. But cell culture removes every step of the dose-loss chain where they actually differ. Lab B's oversized fraction is cleared faster by liver and spleen and extravasates less efficiently. Without PEG, the particles are rapidly opsonized and pulled from circulation. Lab A embodies the design logic behind Doxil — the first FDA-approved nano-drug, approved in 1995. Two particles that look identical in the dish can have opposite fates in the body. Judge a nanomedicine on its predicted biodistribution, not its in-vitro potency.

segments.label: 09 / 12 · EPR — THE CENTRAL QUESTION
title: EPR IN MICE.
EPR IN HUMANS — STILL OPEN.
segments.body_html:
THE PHYSICSLeaky tumor vessels + poor lymphatic drainage = passive accumulation of 10–200 nm particles.
THE MOUSE RECORD~0.7% median delivery. Heavily cited, heavily contested. Mouse tumors are not human tumors.
THE OPEN QUESTIONWhether EPR is consistent enough across human patients to be a reliable design target is an active research question.

beats.text: The physics of the enhanced permeability and retention effect are real: leaky tumor vessels plus poor lymphatic drainage means particles in the right size range can accumulate passively. But the field has learned to treat EPR with caution. The widely cited 0.7 percent delivery figure comes from preclinical mouse data, and human EPR may differ substantially. Mouse tumor models develop different vascular architecture than human tumors, often with more pronounced leakiness. Whether EPR is even consistent enough across human patients to be a reliable engineering design target is one of the field's central contested questions — and the chapter addresses it honestly rather than assuming the mouse-to-human translation holds.

segments.label: 10 / 12 · SEEING PARTICLES
title: LIGHT CANNOT SEE THEM.
ELECTRONS CAN.
segments.body_html:
light · 400–700 nm wavelength→cannot resolve <200 nm
electron beam · pm wavelength→resolves nm-scale features

SEM surveys populations for size and shape statistics. TEM resolves internal structure within a single particle. If you cannot see your particles, you cannot interpret what they did.

beats.text: Characterization requires tools matched to the scale. Dynamic light scattering estimates the size distribution by analyzing how particles scatter a laser beam. But to see the particles directly, you need electron microscopy — because nanoparticles are far smaller than the resolution limit of visible light. Light's wavelength of roughly four hundred to seven hundred nanometers means it physically cannot resolve features smaller than several hundred nanometers. Electron beams at working energies have effective wavelengths thousands of times shorter, resolving nanometer-scale features directly. Scanning electron microscopy surveys populations for shape and size statistics. Transmission electron microscopy resolves internal structure within a single particle. If you cannot see and size your particles, you cannot interpret what they did.

segments.label: 11 / 12 · THE THESIS
title: NANOMEDICINE IS
A DELIVERY DISCIPLINE.
segments.body_html:
The binding constraint is measured biodistribution — not particle elegance. Claims must rest on tracking the particle, not inferring its fate from downstream response.

Still open: whether it will ever be possible to select patients by tumor permeability before treatment — companion diagnostics that change 'build better particles' to 'select better patients.'

beats.text: Here is the chapter's central claim. Nanomedicine is a delivery discipline. The binding constraint is not particle elegance — it is confirmed biodistribution. The field's recurring error is inferring delivery from downstream response: cell death in culture, tumor shrinkage in mice. Neither closes the dose-loss chain. Only tracking the particle itself closes the chain. What would force revision: a large, well-controlled clinical study where particle design alone, independent of confirmed biodistribution, reliably predicted outcome. The existing pattern is the opposite — the variability of tumor delivery is precisely what makes outcomes unpredictable. And still open: whether a companion diagnostic could select patients by tumor permeability before treatment — changing the field from building better particles to selecting better patients.

segments.label: 12 / 12 · CLOSE
title: MEASURE THE JOURNEY.
THEN MAKE THE CLAIM.
segments.body_html:
ENGINEER THE PARTICLE//TRACK ITS BIODISTRIBUTION//CLOSE THE CHAIN

Cancer Nanomedicine · Chapter 1 · What Counts as Cancer Nanomedicine?

beats.text: That is the frame for everything ahead. Cancer nanomedicine succeeds or fails at the level of delivery. Build a particle, yes — but then track where it goes. The 10 to 200 nanometer window opens possibilities that free drug molecules cannot access, but those possibilities only become treatments when the dose-loss chain is actually closed, not assumed closed. Engineer the particle. Track its biodistribution. Measure the journey before you make the claim. Everything in this series is about doing exactly that.
